performers: Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra; Fritz Reiner, conductor
question: How does an orchestral section become a soloist without leaving the ensemble?
intro: A low-string idea grows into a sonata movement in which orchestral sections take turns as soloists. Reiner’s Pittsburgh recording precedes his better-known Chicago remake by nine years.

sections.label: Slow introduction
sections.mNote: low-string fourths expand into an orchestral introduction

sections.label: Fast first group
sections.mNote: the opening fast material establishes the main movement

sections.label: Development begins
sections.mNote: fragments and instrumental exchanges replace a complete statement

sections.label: Quiet development episode
sections.mNote: a retreat within the development, not a new exposition

sections.label: Brass fugato
sections.mNote: overlapping entries rebuild the development’s momentum

sections.label: Lyrical return
sections.mNote: the second group returns before the fast first group

sections.label: Fast closing return
sections.mNote: the first group returns late, reversing the exposition’s order

cues.title: Starting beneath the orchestra
cues.text: The opening idea belongs to cellos and double basses. Its successive fourths leave plenty of space between notes; the upper instruments gradually make that space less empty.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 1–2, opening low-string line and subsequent additions: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Cached analysis bartok-concerto-orchestra-introduzione.txt begins at −48.9 dB and rises over the first 30 seconds. This describes the opening passage, not separately measured instrument entrances.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Keeping the low line
cues.text: As higher sounds become more noticeable, keep the opening’s low line in mind. Bartók lets a background figure remain important after another register has attracted attention.
cues.evidence: Opening scoring, pp. 1–3: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. The report marks a quieter window at 0:35 and a change near 0:40; the listening instruction does not identify a new instrumental attack at 0:36.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: An early gathering of force
cues.text: This early swell makes the introduction sound much larger without yet settling into the main fast movement. Follow its rise and retreat as one gesture.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/bartok-concerto-orchestra-introduzione.txt: level rises from −31.1 dB at 1:10 to −9.8 at 1:25, then falls to −23.2 at 1:35; novelty peaks at 1:18 and 1:34. No chord or instrumental cause is inferred from the measurements.

cues.title: Work after emigration
cues.text: Bartók left Hungary for the United States in October 1940. In New York, work on South Slavic folk-song collections at Columbia University occupied him before this orchestral commission arrived.
cues.evidence: Richard E. Rodda’s Pittsburgh Symphony programme notes, biographical account: https://culturaldistrict-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/culturaldistrict/system/assets/29105/original/Jan._17-19__2020.pdf. Contextual placement, not a programme attached to the notes sounding here.

cues.title: A commission in memory
cues.text: Serge Koussevitzky commissioned the work in memory of his wife, Natalie. Reiner and the violinist Joseph Szigeti helped bring Bartók’s circumstances to the conductor’s attention.
cues.evidence: Rodda, commission account: https://culturaldistrict-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/culturaldistrict/system/assets/29105/original/Jan._17-19__2020.pdf. No claim that a specific musical theme portrays either patron.

cues.title: The fast movement takes hold
cues.text: After the spacious introduction, the Allegro vivace gives the music a more continuous drive. Listen for the difference between a sustained orchestral call and a short figure that can be passed on.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 5–8, Allegro vivace from bar 76: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. The estimated section anchor is the strong 2:54 novelty peak; 2:55–3:20 contains sustained high relative levels. Passage alignment is approximate, not a bar-exact claim.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An ensemble of soloists
cues.text: Here “concerto” does not mean one player standing apart from the orchestra. Listen for a whole instrumental section taking the foreground, then surrendering it to another group.
cues.evidence: Bartók’s explanation of the title is quoted by Rodda: https://culturaldistrict-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/culturaldistrict/system/assets/29105/original/Jan._17-19__2020.pdf. Score pp. 5–12 shows the exchanges: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. This is a movement-wide listening invitation, not an audio-separated identification at 3:50.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Room for a longer phrase
cues.text: The quieter contrasting span makes room for a more sustained line. Compare its breathing with the short, forceful figures of the fast opening group.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 9–11, Tranquillo material from bar 155: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. The report places a lower-level stretch around 4:15–4:40, including −23.3 dB at 4:20. The second-group anchor at 4:10 is approximate; no soloist onset is claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Material becomes an argument
cues.text: In the development, a familiar idea need not return as a complete tune. Listen for fragments, changed accompaniment and one group answering another: identity can survive a change of scale.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 12–19, development from Tempo I around bar 231: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. The estimated 4:58 anchor follows novelty peaks at 4:42 and 4:58 and precedes renewed activity. Formal placement is approximate, not derived from machine key labels.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Uneven pressure
cues.text: The development does not simply grow louder at a steady rate. Short rises and withdrawals keep altering the weight of the argument before its larger accumulation.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/bartok-concerto-orchestra-introduzione.txt: novelty peaks at 5:28, 5:44 and 5:58; level moves from −17.3 dB at 5:30 through −23.7 at 5:50 to −10.6 at 6:05. These measurements support a changing contour, not a harmonic analysis.

cues.title: Pittsburgh before Chicago
cues.text: This is Reiner’s Pittsburgh recording, made in February 1946 and first issued in 1948. His familiar Chicago account is a different performance, recorded for RCA in October 1955.
cues.evidence: Klára Móricz, source RecR: https://www.henle.de/media/7c/05/ab/1697725629/7001-1697725628-sync.pdf . Chicago Symphony Archives dates the later recording to 22 October 1955: https://chicagosymphony.org/inside-the-music/article/8311/125-moments-011-first-grammy-awards . The selected file’s stored fingerprint also attributes it to Pittsburgh: https://acoustid.org/track/b8fae331-f366-4440-a599-e9f7e08c92c8 .

cues.title: A retreat before the surge
cues.text: The sound has become markedly quieter. Keep listening through this inward stretch: it separates two stages of the development rather than ending the movement’s argument.
cues.evidence: The report falls from −15.2 dB at 6:30 to −31.6 at 6:35 and remains relatively quiet through 7:10. Score pp. 15–16 supplies the quieter developmental episode: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. This is a passage-level placement.

cues.title: Entries that overlap
cues.text: The brass fugato builds by letting one entry begin before another has finished. Follow the accumulating lines rather than hearing the brass as a single block of sound.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 17–19, imitative brass writing from bar 313: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. The report records renewed level and onset activity after 7:15, including 3.8 onsets/s at 7:30 and 4.2 at 7:50. Instrument identity comes from the score; the 7:15 map anchor is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The gentler idea returns first
cues.text: Bartók reverses the order of the principal groups on their return. The more lyrical material comes back before the fast first group, so the later part of the movement does not simply replay its earlier route.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 20–24: Tranquillo at bar 396 precedes the late first-group return around bar 476: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Novelty peaks at 8:12 and a drop from −9.2 dB at 8:05 to −27.9 at 8:15 anchor the approximate lyrical return.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The quietest preparation
cues.text: The returning lyrical span withdraws before the last fast push. Notice how the low level leaves the renewed movement room to grow, rather than announcing the ending at full strength.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/bartok-concerto-orchestra-introduzione.txt: novelty at 8:50, level −35.3 dB at 8:55, then −30.1 at 9:00 and −25.4 at 9:05. The measurements locate the withdrawal and renewed rise, not an exact first note.

cues.title: A late concentration of energy
cues.text: The final fast span gathers force towards the closing bars. Compare this concentrated finish with the long time the opening needed to gather an orchestra around its low-string idea.
cues.evidence: The report rises from −24.0 dB at 9:10 to −10.0 at 9:45 before the final decay. Score pp. 24–28 supplies the closing fast return: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. This is a broad closing contour, not a timestamped cadence identification.

transitions.title: Sustained space becomes continuous motion
transitions.how: The introduction’s spacious calls give way to the Allegro vivace. Short, mobile figures can now circulate between groups instead of waiting above a slowly unfolding bass. The contrast is a change of pace and texture, not a silent break between two independent pieces.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 5, bar 76: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Strongest early novelty peak at 2:54; level rises sharply from −24.1 dB at 2:50 to −9.3 at 2:55. Approximate passage alignment.

transitions.title: The line lengthens as force recedes
transitions.how: The first group’s forceful exchanges subside into Tranquillo writing. A more sustained wind line and lighter accompaniment replace the short foreground gestures. The pulse remains present beneath the longer phrase; contrast comes from pacing and orchestral weight rather than a complete stop.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 9–11, bar 155 onward: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Lower-level span around 4:15–4:40 supports the approximate 4:10 anchor; this is not a precise solo entrance.

transitions.title: Statements give way to fragments
transitions.how: After the exposition’s more sustained material, the renewed Tempo I turns attention towards smaller figures and exchanges between parts. Familiar shapes become material for continuation rather than a melody to be repeated intact. The texture starts to accumulate again after the quieter close.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 12, bar 231 and following: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Novelty at 4:42 and 4:58, with a low level around 4:50 followed by a rise, supplies approximate anchors.

transitions.title: The argument changes scale
transitions.how: The busier developmental texture retreats into a more exposed, lyrical episode. A thinner accompaniment lets a wind phrase carry the argument without the earlier orchestral weight. This is a local withdrawal inside the development, not a return to the beginning of the movement.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 15–16, Tranquillo and wind-led continuation: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Level drops from −15.2 dB at 6:30 to −31.6 at 6:35; estimated passage boundary 6:35.

transitions.title: One entry recruits another
transitions.how: The quieter episode leads to an imitative build. Brass entries overlap, making a growing texture from a recognisable figure rather than presenting a new song. Renewed rhythmic activity and accumulating voices restore the development’s forward pressure.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 17–19, from bar 313: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Reported level rises from −27.3 dB at 7:10 to −15.8 at 7:15, with higher onset activity thereafter. Exact brass entrances are not measured.

transitions.title: Accumulation releases into song
transitions.how: The developmental accumulation gives way to the quieter second group. Bartók recovers its longer line before returning to the fast first group. That reversed order lets the lyrical material provide relief now while reserving the more urgent material for the close.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 20, Tranquillo at bar 396: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Novelty peak 8:12 and sharp level reduction between 8:05 and 8:15 support this approximate return.

transitions.title: The reserved first group returns
transitions.how: The lyrical return thins and the movement accelerates into its late recovery of the first group. The mobile material can now lead straight towards the ending. Instead of another complete exposition, Bartók concentrates the remaining energy into this closing return.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 24–28, acceleration and late first-group return around bar 476: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Quiet minimum at 8:55 followed by a sustained rise after 9:00 anchors the approximate boundary.

source.title: Bartók, Concerto for Orchestra, B. & H. 9009, I
source.locator: Printed pp. 1–28. Viewed 1946-edition scan; broad snapshots of scored passages, approximately aligned to the measured section anchors. Allow roughly 10 seconds around a change. Not instrument recognition or a claim to reconstruct Reiner’s corrected manuscript note for note.

timeline.note: The opening fourth-based idea begins in the low strings (p. 1).
Across the opening expansion, flute figures contrast with muted, divided strings (pp. 1–2).
Brass calls expand the introduction above low-string motion; a passage snapshot, not a precisely timed attack (pp. 2–4).
The fast first group puts mobile strings in the foreground with wind and horn responses (pp. 5–8).
The Tranquillo region exchanges wind phrases above restrained strings, horn harmony and harp (pp. 9–11).
Different wind colours share the quiet developmental episode over strings; not all listed winds play continuously (pp. 15–16).
Imitative brass entries accumulate through the fugato, supported and answered by strings (pp. 17–19).
The returning lyrical material passes through exposed wind writing above lighter accompaniment (pp. 20–23).
Fast string material regains the foreground and recruits the wind and brass sections towards the closing tutti (pp. 24–28).

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The Archive explicitly identifies Pittsburgh, 1946. Its stored AcoustID resolves to a Pittsburgh/Reiner recording, corroborating that attribution rather than merely comparing durations. This is not the Chicago Symphony/RCA recording of 22 October 1955. The fingerprint database is supplementary, community-maintained evidence, not a fresh comparison performed here.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral version; Reiner’s corrected conducting score, with Bartók’s revised finale ending.
fields.note: Móricz identifies the performing source as Reiner’s tissue proof CR, corrected by Bartók, and explicitly associates the 1946 recording with the new ending. The 1946 printed score is consulted for broad orchestration, not represented as Reiner’s exact performing copy; minor textual differences are not timed here. The Archive description mistakenly gives BB 127, which belongs to Piano Concerto No. 3.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The critical edition identifies this range for the complete recording. The Sony discographical transcription gives 5 February for CD 5 tracks 1–5; individual movement/session allocation is not established. Neither the 1948 issue nor 2010 upload is a session date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Venue stated in the reproduced Columbia session discography. No microphone position or engineer is established for the selected transfer.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: This identifies the original commercial recording, not the unidentified physical or digital carrier from which the Archive MP3 was copied.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The discographical transcription dates MM-793 to 22 November 1948 and ML 4102 to 7 February 1949. Douglas Watt’s March 1949 review independently identifies Columbia set 793 and ML-4102 as the same Pittsburgh/Reiner performance. The exact carrier used by public-domain-archive.com remains unknown; no sleeve or label scans accompany the selected Archive item.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Complete set: XCO 35800–35811, take 1; LP matrices xLP 539 (I–II), xLP 540 (III–V)
fields.note: These are complete-recording identifiers transcribed from Sony’s discography, not an asserted side-by-side mapping for this MP3. Individual movement matrix boundaries, transfer-side joins and the transferred pressing are unknown. DAHR’s opened Reiner listing does not include these Columbia masters; no DAHR matrix record is fabricated.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: Archive says only that the files were taken from public-domain-archive.com. Neither transfer engineer nor restoration producer is named. The uploader is not treated as the transfer engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Archive public date, 8 August 2010, and file modification dates describe repository activity, not the date of analogue transfer or mastering.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: Original digitisation, equalisation, noise reduction, editing, speed correction and the source carrier are unestablished. The item calls the selected file an original VBR MP3 and supplies Ogg derivatives; this does not identify how the historical master was transferred.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public domain in the EU under the ordinary life-plus-70 term; not a worldwide clearance.
fields.note: Bartók died in 1945; IMSLP identifies this score as public domain in life-plus-70 countries and explicitly warns of continuing US protection. The critical-edition commentary is cited as scholarship, not redistributed as a public-domain score.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: first lawful publication in 1948, before 1963.
fields.note: Móricz’s source RecR states first released in 1948; the Columbia discography identifies MM-793 and its 22 November 1948 issue. A contemporary March 1949 review independently establishes that the recording was commercially available as Columbia set 793 and ML-4102. This is a publication basis anywhere, not an assumption from the 1946 session. Its former 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension. US sound-recording status is not established. The Archive’s legacy public-domain URL alone is not relied upon; it is an uploader declaration, not proof of the performers’ release.

composer.born: 25 March 1881, Nagyszentmiklós, Hungary (now Sânnicolau Mare, Romania)
composer.epithet: A pianist and fieldworker who turned the modes, rhythms and performance habits of peasant music into new kinds of quartet and orchestral argument.
facts: Budapest Academy of Music, 1899–1903: piano with István Thomán, composition with Hans Koessler
Piano professor, Budapest Academy, 1907–34 · Hungarian Academy of Sciences folk-music project, 1934–40 · Columbia University research in American exile
Hungarian, Slovak and Romanian villages · Biskra, Algeria, 1913 · Turkey, 1936
Six string quartets · three piano concertos · two violin concertos · three stage works · folk-music collections and pedagogical music
composer.background:
Bartók was born in Nagyszentmiklós, a town in the Hungarian half of Austria-Hungary which became part of Romania after the First World War. His father, who directed an agricultural school, died in 1888; his mother, Paula Voit, supported Béla and his sister by teaching. After several moves the family settled in Pozsony, now Bratislava. The changing names on this map matter: the Hungarian, Slovak and Romanian communities he later recorded occupied overlapping musical territories. His professional education began within the German-speaking conservatoire tradition.

At the Budapest Academy from 1899 to 1903, he studied piano with István Thomán, a pupil of Liszt, and composition with Hans Koessler. Hearing Richard Strauss’s Also sprach Zarathustra in 1902 helped release him from student exercises. Kossuth, composed in 1903, made the Hungarian revolutionary leader the subject of a large orchestral narrative and caricatured Haydn’s imperial anthem as the Austrian enemy. This early nationalist programme preceded the comparative research that would complicate his understanding of national music.
